request.system:
You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader. Write Markdown only, never HTML.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Add nothing to a fact: no benefit, cause, consequence or comparison it does not state itself, however likely it seems. If a fact says the strainer has two ears, do not write that the ears rest on the mug's rim; if a fact says a tin holds 100 g of tea, do not write that a 60 g bag fits in it; if a fact says the grinder has 30 settings, do not write that this makes it easy to dial in. State the fact plainly, and put any general advice in its own sentence that does not name the product.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

{"title":"How to Make Your Dog Visible at Night: Safety Tips for Dark Evening Walks","meta_description":"Learn how to make your dog visible at night with clip-on lights, reflective gear, good leash control and a simple checklist for safer dark evening walks.","slug":"how-to-make-your-dog-visible-at-night","markdown":"The best way to make your dog visible at night is to layer up. Put an active light on their collar or harness so they glow from every angle. Add reflective gear that bounces headlights back to drivers. Keep your dog close and under control on a short leash, and make sure you are easy to spot too. Here's how to put that kit together so your dark evening walks feel calm and safe.

## Why dogs disappear in the dark

Dogs are surprisingly hard to see once the sun goes down. Many have dark or brindled coats that blend into tarmac, hedges and shadows. They are also low to the ground, below the line where drivers, cyclists and runners naturally look. Car headlights are aimed at the road ahead, so a dog at the edge of a lane or crossing a driveway is often only noticed at the last moment.

It helps to understand the two ways of being seen:

- **Being lit (active light):** a light source on your dog that shines on its own. It can be seen whether or not anyone is pointing a light at it, and from any direction.
- **Being reflective (passive):** materials that only shine when light hits them, such as headlights or a torch beam. They work well on roads, but on a dark path with no light around they don't help much.

The safest setup uses both. A light makes your dog visible all the time, and reflective gear gives an extra boost when a car or bike comes along.

## Light them up: using a clip-on LED light

An active light is the single most effective step you can take, because it doesn't depend on anyone else's light source. It also helps *you* keep track of your dog when they wander a little ahead or sniff around in the dark.

Our [Rechargeable LED Collar Light](P1) clips onto any collar or harness [F1]. It is visible from about 1,000 ft [F3].

{{P1}}

### Where to attach it

As a general rule, attach a light where it sits high and isn't hidden by fur or a jacket. The top of the collar or the back of a harness tends to be visible from the sides and from above. If your dog has a long, fluffy coat, check that the light isn't buried after a good shake.

### Steady or flashing?

The collar light has three modes: steady, slow flash and fast flash [F2]. As general guidance, a steady light can make it easier to follow your dog's movements on a quiet path or in a park. A flashing light tends to stand out more against streetlights, shop windows and traffic, so many owners switch to a flashing mode near roads.

### Battery, charging and wet weather

A light is only useful if it's actually on, so it's worth thinking about power before you leave the house. The collar light is rechargeable and charges via USB-C [F8, F4]. It runs for 6 hours on steady mode [F5]. It is also rated IPX7 waterproof [F6]. Getting into the habit of charging it at the same time each day means it is always ready for the evening walk.

## Add reflective gear for headlight visibility

Reflective materials work by bouncing light straight back towards its source. When a car's headlights hit a reflective strip, the driver sees a bright flash right where your dog is. That makes reflective gear a great backup layer: if your light runs out or gets knocked off, you still have something working for you near traffic.

Our [Front-Clip No-Pull Harness](P2) is a harness with reflective stitching [F9, F15]. Reflective details on a harness, collar or leash add up, so it's worth looking for them across all of your dog's walking kit. You can browse everything in our [walking gear collection](L1).

Keep in mind that reflective gear is passive. On an unlit footpath with no traffic, it won't do much on its own, which is why pairing it with a light is the way to go.

## Keep control when visibility is low

Being seen is only half the job. At night, a dog that suddenly lunges at a fox, a cat or another dog can end up in the road before a driver has time to react. Good control matters even more when everyone's view is limited.

### How a front-clip harness helps

The Front-Clip No-Pull Harness has a leash ring on the chest that turns the dog sideways when it pulls [F12]. It also has a padded neoprene chest plate [F14]. If you're weighing up different styles, our guide on [how to choose a dog harness](L3) walks through the options.

{{P2}}

### Get the fit right

A harness that slips or twists won't give you the control you need, so take a few minutes to get the fit right. The Front-Clip No-Pull Harness has four adjustment points [F13]. It comes in sizes XS, S, M, L and XL, fitting a chest girth of 13–42 in across the range [F11, F16]. Measure your dog's chest at the widest point and check our [harness size guide](L6) before choosing a size.

As a general check, you should be able to slide a couple of fingers under the straps, and the harness shouldn't rub behind the front legs or slide around when your dog moves.

### Stick to a standard-length leash near roads

Long lines are brilliant for recall training in open fields, but they're not a good fit for dark streets. A long trailing line is hard to see, easy to trip over and gives your dog room to reach the road before you can react. Near traffic, a standard-length leash keeps your dog close enough to guide. Our [dog leash length guide](L4) explains when each length makes sense.

## Make yourself visible too

Your dog is attached to you, so if drivers can see you, they're more likely to notice your dog as well. A few simple habits make a big difference:

- **Carry a headlamp or torch.** It lights up the ground ahead, helps you spot hazards (and anything your dog shouldn't eat), and makes you visible to others.
- **Wear bright or reflective clothing.** A reflective vest, armband or jacket with reflective panels helps drivers pick you out in their headlights.
- **Walk facing traffic where there's no pavement.** You'll see oncoming cars sooner and can step in with your dog on the side away from the road.
- **Choose well-lit routes when you can.** Streetlit roads and busy paths are easier for everyone than dark country lanes.

## A quick night-walk checklist

Before you head out on a dark evening, run through this quick list:

1. **Charge the light.** Plug the collar light in via USB-C during the day so it's ready to go [F4].
2. **Clip it on.** Attach the collar light to your dog's collar or harness and switch it on before you leave [F1].
3. **Check the harness and reflective gear.** Make sure the harness fits snugly and its reflective stitching isn't covered by a coat or jacket [F15].
4. **Use a short leash.** Save the long line for daytime training in open spaces.
5. **Choose a well-lit route.** Stick to lit streets and familiar paths where you can.
6. **Carry a torch and wear something bright.** Make sure drivers can see you as clearly as your dog.

With a light, a bit of reflective gear and a well-fitted harness, dark evenings don't have to cut your walks short. Set up the kit once, make charging part of your routine, and you and your dog can enjoy those winter strolls with a lot more confidence."}
